stature.source: typical and tall: the Gymnosperm Database's 24-46 m, the drafter centring on the Olympic silver fir zone; record: 71.9 m, East Fork Humptulips River, Olympic National Forest, last seen 1999 (Gymnosperm Database); read 2026-11-04

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-04), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a dense, narrow, very dark spire on a smooth pale-grey trunk; old trees become cylindrical and flat-topped

young.note: a sapling in deep shade, flat sprays of dark needles in tiers, waiting for a gap

old-growth.note: an old tree with a flat-topped, cylindrical crown and bark breaking into reddish-grey scaly plates

description: The shade-loving fir of the Olympics' middle slopes, 30-50 m here, a dense, dark, narrow spire on a smooth, pale-grey trunk dotted with resin blisters. Its needles are a deep glossy green above and brilliant silvery-white beneath, so the forest flashes silver when wind turns the boughs.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen under deep, wet snow; the dense tiers hold it.
season_notes.spring: Shoots break late in pale green tufts; red pollen cones under the branches.
season_notes.summer: Upright, resinous purple cones 8-10 cm sit on the top branches.
season_notes.fall: The cones fall apart on the branch, leaving bare spikes; seedlings carpet the shaded duff.

range.where: the Pacific silver fir zone of the Olympics, about 600-1,200 m on the west side, higher in the east; at sea level in the wettest western valleys and up to the subalpine; Alaska to the Oregon Cascades, a few stands in far northern California

notes: A fir grown from Douglas-fir: needles single and flat (the template's needle_flat cards are close), 1-2.5 cm, those on top of the twig pressed forward and covering it, and cones upright and shattering, unlike the template's hanging ones (not expressed). The colour is the point: very dark glossy green above, silver-white below (Gymnosperm Database); the summer colour is the dark top side as seen from the ground, and the silver flash of the undersides in wind is not drawn (a two-sided needle colour would carry it). Young trees are smooth, light grey with resin blisters; old ones break into reddish-grey scaly plates. It is among the most shade-tolerant conifers and very intolerant of fire (Gymnosperm Database). Douglas squirrels and grosbeaks take the seed, sooty grouse the needles, and elk and deer browse the saplings lightly in winter; only the deer and Steller's jay are in the animal library.
sources: The Gymnosperm Database, Abies amabilis, https://www.conifers.org/pi/Abies_amabilis.php, read 2026-11-04
